confidence_why: 8 independent first-hand descriptions agree (4 state the same rule, 3 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: penultimate vowel lengthening, which we take to be a form of phrasal stress which occurs at the right edge of every prosodic phrase.
sweep_summary: Nine title hits searched for Zulu (catalog: fixed-dominant, phrasal penult lengthening as stress; deciding sources Cope 1966 / Wu & Gowda 2020, checked 9/16). Two open copies downloaded and read: Downing 1990 (SAL 21(3), open access) and Cheng & Downing 2007 (SOAS WPL 15, via an Internet Archive copy since the live SOAS page is 404 and Leiden blocks our network). Both confirm penult lengthening as the stress/prominence cue of the phrase-final word; Downing 1990 additionally makes explicit that the antepenult 'accent' of the Nguni tone-shift literature (Clark 1988, Goldsmith/Peterson/Drogo, Downing's own rule (8)) is an abstract tonal attractor distinct from stress, which refines but does not change the classification. Downing 2007 (ICPhS satellite talk) has no surviving copy but is the held Downing 2008 ZASPiL paper. Not readable: Halpert 2017 (De Gruyter; author Drive copy needs sign-in), Clark 1988 (De Gruyter; archive.org lending only), Roux 1995 (T&F, an automated-access block), Downing 2010 and von Staden 1977 (print only). Hall 1995 is archaeology (keyword false positive). Nothing found supersedes the catalog's deciding source; the only items worth acquiring are Roux 1995 (possible instrumental data on penult length vs stress) and von Staden 1977 (prosody of ideophones, the one class Khumalo 1987 assigns lexical stress). all look-ups went through direct API/automated download and direct download.

new_statements.quote: The derivation of a falling contour from the representation in (59b) seems to be triggered by stress-induced lengthening of the penult. Although I have not indicated this in the transcriptions, phrase-penult syllables are lengthened in Nguni as in many other Southern Bantu languages [Doke 1954], so the falling contour (the phrase-final tone pattern) is realized only on lengthened penults.
new_statements.citation: Downing, Laura J. 1990. Local and metrical tone shift in Nguni. Studies in African Linguistics 21(3): 261-317. doi:10.32473/sal.v21i3.107431
new_statements.reading: Stress in Zulu (Nguni) is realized as lengthening of the phrase-penult syllable; the metrical 'accent' that attracts High tones (antepenult phrase-finally, rule (8) p. 268; penult if high-toned, p. 286) is a separate, tonal prominence and is not what the length/stress facts track. Corroborated first-hand by Cheng & Downing 2007: 52, where the phrase penult vowel's lengthening is 'the primary prosodic correlate' of Durban Zulu phrasing. Both agree with the catalog's fixed-dominant (penult, phrasal) coding and with the held Cope 1966, Khumalo 1987, Downing 2008 and Wu & Gowda 2020.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction. Refinement only: the stronger stress locator in the same file is p. 310 (p. 50), sec. 3.2 end: "As in most Southern Bantu languages [Doke 1954], the penultimate syllable is lengthened in Nguni (most noticeably phrase-finally) due to regular stress on that syllable.. the unstressed antepenult.. non-contrastive, stress-induced vowel length only in the penult." That passage states regular penult stress at word level (most noticeable phrase-finally), which matches the Cope 1966 / Doke word-penult coding even more directly than the p. 304 phrase-penult remark.

It refines the catalog by (a) stating the word-level rule flatly ('always on the penultimate syllable'), (b) making the phrase-final conditioning of prominence explicit (a non-phrase-final penult is 'non-prominent'), and (c) documenting that Wh enclitics incorporate and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is always on the penultimate syllable. The stressed penult is realized as a lengthened, prominent syllable only when the word is phrase-final ('prepausal lengthening', p. 65: 'a penultimate syllable is lengthened before a certain prosodic boundary'); the penult of a non-phrase-final word (e.g. the short present-tense verb form) is 'non-prominent'. High tone avoids the prominent (lengthened, stressed) penult, so a shifting High stops on the antepenult phrase-finally but goes all the way to the penult phrase-medially. Wh enclitics (-phi 'where', -ni 'what') incorporate into the preceding verb and stress shifts rightward to the syllable immediately before the enclitic, i.e. the stress domain is verb+enclitic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in Zulu. The one mention of 'secondary penultimate stress' (p. 11, p. 23) concerns the material preceding the macrostem in a Swahili synthetic relative (example (12b)), not Zulu.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitic incorporation moves stress onto the syllable before the enclitic (p. 144, examples (255)). Prepausal lengthening applies only at a prosodic (IP) boundary (pp. 65-66, fn. 13 'This description is somewhat simplified'); a lengthened short verb form is treated as ungrammatical or at least unnatural (fn. 14, p. 66, citing van der Spuy 1993 for Zulu and Jokweni 1995 for Xhosa).
new_statements.identity_note: Buell's data are standard Zulu (he notes the standard is 'based on the Natal (southeast coast) dialect', p. 7) from his own informant plus published sources; he states that Xhosa 'will be treated essentially as a dialect of Zulu in this discussion' (p. 7), and some of the prepausal-lengthening judgments cited in fn. 14 (Jokweni 1995) are Xhosa, not Zulu. The stress statements quoted are about Zulu itself.

sources.citation: Cheng, Lisa Lai-Shen & Laura J. Downing. 2007. The prosody and syntax of Zulu relative clauses. SOAS Working Papers in Linguistics 15: 51-63.
sources.quote: Our study of Durban Zulu prosodic phrasing shows that Jokweni's (1995) findings for Xhosa, shown in (1), find a parallel, for the most part, in Durban Zulu. The primary prosodic correlate of the phrasing is that the phrase penult vowel is lengthened. In some tonal contexts, we also see tonal alternations conditioned by prosodic phrasing. For example, 'children' is often realized with a High tone through the penult - ábá-ntwána.... - phrase-medially, but with a High tone only through the antepenult - ábá-ntwa:na - phrase-finally.
sources.note: Fieldwork on Durban Zulu (consultant Meritta Xaba): the one consistent prosodic correlate of phrasing is lengthening of the phrase-penult vowel; the paper is about prosodic phrasing of relative clauses and never uses the word stress, so it confirms the phrasal-penult prominence the catalog codes but adds nothing on word-level stress.
